v.q: What is the main benefit of putting a message broker between two services?
o: The producer does not wait for the consumer to be running
Every call becomes synchronous and ordered
Retries are no longer needed anywhere
Messages are guaranteed never to repeat
v.w: Producers and consumers can scale and fail independently, and the broker buffers bursts.

v.q: Which situation is a benefit of asynchronous messaging?
o: The consumer can be offline
Every call returns at once
Messages never repeat
No retries are needed
v.w: The broker stores messages, so producer and consumer do not have to run at the same time.

v.q: What is the difference between a queue and a topic (publish/subscribe)?
o: A queue delivers each message to one consumer, a topic to every subscriber
A queue carries text while a topic carries binary data
A topic keeps messages forever while a queue keeps none
The two are the same thing under different names
v.w: Queues share work between competing consumers. Topics broadcast events to independent subscribers, each with its own position or queue.

v.q: Which statement about queues and topics is NOT true?
o: A queue delivers each message to every consumer
A topic delivers to every subscriber
A queue shares messages among competing consumers
Each consumer group gets its own copy in Kafka
v.w: A queue gives each message to one consumer. Fan-out is the job of a topic.

v.q: Which delivery guarantee is the realistic default for most brokers?
o: At-least-once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates
Exactly-once end to end with no extra work
At-most-once with guaranteed delivery
Exactly-once for free between any two systems
v.w: Acknowledge after processing and a crash causes redelivery. Make consumers idempotent, for example by tracking message ids.

v.q: Which handling of duplicate delivery is correct for a payment consumer?
o: Make the handler idempotent
Assume it never happens
Ignore failures
Process twice to be safe
v.w: At-least-once delivery means a message can arrive again, so a repeat must not charge twice.

v.q: A consumer keeps failing on one malformed message. What stops it blocking the queue?
o: Retry a few times, then park it in a dead-letter queue
Retry for ever without waiting between the attempts
Delete the message silently so nobody ever sees it
Restart the broker every few minutes until it works
v.w: A dead-letter queue parks poison messages for inspection and replay. Retries should use backoff.

v.q: Which practice with a poison message is NOT sensible?
o: Retry it forever with no pause
Move it to a dead-letter queue
Retry with backoff a few times
Alert on messages in the DLQ
v.w: Endless retry blocks the queue and wastes resources. A DLQ keeps the message for inspection.

v.q: Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only within a partition?
o: Each partition is an ordered log read by one consumer in a group
Kafka sorts all messages by their timestamp
Every topic is limited to a single broker
The producer's clock enforces the ordering
v.w: Use a key (for example the account id) so all related events go to the same partition and stay in order.

v.q: Which Kafka design choice keeps all events of one account in order?
o: Use the account id as the message key
Use a random key
Use many partitions with no key
Send each event to its own topic
v.w: The same key goes to the same partition, and a partition is an ordered log.

o: Slowing or limiting producers when consumers fall behind
Encrypting messages when the system is under load
Deleting the oldest messages first
Raising the replica count of the topic
v.w: Without it queues grow without bound. Options include bounded queues, rate limits, pull-based consumption and scaling consumers.

v.q: Which technique limits the damage when consumers cannot keep up with producers?
o: Backpressure
Larger messages
More producers
No monitoring
v.w: The system must slow producers or reject work, or the queue grows without bound.

v.q: A service updates its database and then publishes an event. It crashes between the two steps. Which pattern solves this?
o: Transactional outbox: save the event in the same database transaction
Publish first and update the database a little afterwards
Use a much longer timeout on the publish call itself
Send the same event twice just to be on the safe side
v.w: The two systems cannot share one transaction. The outbox makes the event part of the local commit and a relay publishes it, with at-least-once delivery.

v.q: Which statement about the transactional outbox is NOT true?
o: It publishes before the database commit
It stores the event in the same transaction
A relay publishes the stored events
Consumers may see a duplicate
v.w: The event is stored with the data and published afterwards, so no crash can separate the two.

v.q: What is a consumer group in Kafka?
o: Consumers sharing a group id divide the topic's partitions
A set of brokers that hold replicas of a topic
A group of producers that write in order
A list of topic names a client may use
v.w: Different groups each receive the full stream. Within one group each partition is read by only one member at a time.

v.q: Three consumers join one Kafka group on a topic with six partitions. How are partitions assigned?
o: Two partitions to each consumer
All six to one consumer
All six to each consumer
One each, three unused
v.w: Within a group each partition belongs to one consumer, and the partitions are divided between them.
